clinicalPearls: Headache caused by sustained external pressure or traction on the scalp or forehead without skin damage
The compression form follows a tight band, hat, helmet or swimming goggles pressing on the head
The traction form follows sustained pulling, as from tightly tied-back hair
Pain is maximal at the site of pressure or traction and generally resolves after the stimulus is removed
It can trigger a migraine attack in susceptible individuals
Management is simply avoiding or relieving the offending external force
reference.pathophysiology: External-pressure headache results from continuous mechanical stimulation of cutaneous nerves and pericranial structures by pressure or traction on the scalp, activating trigeminal and cervical sensory afferents to produce localised pain. It is a benign response to an external physical stimulus rather than intrinsic intracranial pathology, although in migraine-prone individuals the peripheral input can act as a trigger for a full migraine attack.
additionalDifferentials: Contact dermatitis or local skin pathology causing pain
additionalInvestigations: Clinical diagnosis from the clear relationship to external pressure or traction
Examination confirming pain localised to the compressed or tractioned site
Investigation only if features are atypical or persist after removing the stimulus
redFlags: Headache persisting well beyond removal of the pressure or traction
Associated skin breakdown or infection at the site
A new or progressive headache pattern unrelated to external force
reference.prognosis: The condition is benign and resolves once the external pressure or traction is removed; recurrence is easily prevented by avoiding the trigger.
pitfalls: Overlooking a simple mechanical cause and pursuing unnecessary investigation
Confusing it with tension-type or cervicogenic headache
Missing that it has triggered a migraine in a susceptible person
Ignoring recurrent occupational causes such as protective headgear
references: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: Remove or loosen the offending external force, such as a tight hat, helmet, headband or swimming goggles, which relieves the pain
Relieve traction headache by undoing tightly tied-back hair
Prevent recurrence by adjusting headwear and hairstyle to avoid sustained scalp pressure or traction
Reassure the patient about the benign, self-limiting nature of the headache
In migraine-prone individuals, avoid the external trigger to prevent it precipitating a full migraine attack
Investigate further only if features are atypical or the headache persists after the stimulus is removed
